newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk-Iran gas line construction to start in March.
newsitem.headline: Turk-Iran gas line construction to start in March.

text.p: Turkey and Iran will start construction in March of a natural gas pipeline to carry Iranian gas to Turkey, Turkish Energy Minister Recai Kutan said on Tuesday.

"Iran and Turkey will lay the ground at the same time for the construction of the gas pipeline in March at the joint border," he told reporters during a joint news conference with the visiting Iranian Oil Minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh in Ankara.

"The pipeline will carry three billion cubic metres of Iranian gas from the beginning of 1998, one year earlier than the original project," he said. "Later from 2005 the purchases will be 10 billion cubic metres."
He said both Iran and Turkey would invite tenders separately later this month to build the segments of the pipeline in their territories.
"We will give the contractor consortia two months to submit their bids and later assess the bids for one month. We will choose the contractor in March, when the construction will begin," he said.

He said Turkey would initially tender for the 250-km (156-mile) part from the border to its eastern province of Erzurum and Iran for the 270-km (169-mile) segment from Tabriz to the Turkish border. Both lines will be 40 inches in diameter.
"The initial part in Turkey will cost about $200 million and so will the part in Iran. Both countries will finance the pipeline projects themselves," he said.

Turkey will later hold another tender after the Iranian gas reached Erzurum to carry it to Ankara through a 800-km (500-mile) pipeline whose capacity will be determined after talks for 16 billion cubic metres a year more of gas fro Russia through its eastern border have been finalised.
"The Russian gas, if agreed, will also reach Erzurum through a pipeline from Georgia to Erzurum. Therefore a larger line may be needed for Erzurum-Ankara segment," Kutan said.
He said some gas-fired power plants would be built along the line and gas would be used for several industrial sites and homes in the economically backward cities in the east.
Aghazadeh said Turkey's payments for gas would be in cash but both ministers refused to disclose the exact price.
"The (two-way) trade volume between Turkey and Iran is planned to rise to $2 billion a year and Turkey's payments will be included in this amount," Aghazadeh said.
Kutan said the price would "not be against our national interests."
Kutan said Turkey would continue to buy about five million tonnes of crude from its eastern neighbour.
Aghazadeh said the religious brothers Turkey and Iran would also cooperate in projects that they may undertake in third countries, especially in Africa and Asia.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist coalition government, which signed the $23-billion, 23-year gas agreement in Tehran in August, vowed to improve Turkey's relations with Islamic countries, and especially with Iran.
Kutan said the gas deal would not breach a U.S. law that non-U.S. investors putting at least $40 million in energy projects in Iran and Libya would be punished.
He slammed comments by U.S. State Department Spokesman Nicholas Burns that the U.S. did "not believe it is a good idea for any country to have normal relations with Iran."

"America made its suggestion. That's fine. But we need energy and go ahead according to our national interests," said Kutan, a member of the Islamist wing of the coalition. "I myself don't believe Iran is a terrorist country."
Under the gas deal Iran will have sold about 190 billion cubic metres to Turkey in the lifetime of the project.
Kutan and Aghazadeh, who will leave Ankara on Wednesday, signed a memorandum of understanding to determine the details of the gas deal and to implement it.
Kutan said Turkey's annual gas demand would shoot up to 27 billion cubic metres in 2000 from the present nine billion. It would rise to 38 billion cubic metres in 2005 and 52 billion in 2010.
-- Ercan Ersoy, Ankara Newsroom +90 312 4462940
